claims.text: Protective oxide formation in high-temperature HEAs is governed by selective oxidation of reactive elements such as Al and Cr.
Al and Cr preferentially form Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3 in the disordered HEA matrix.
The resulting protective oxide is thin, dense, and adherent.
A protective oxide layer limits further oxygen ingress and outward metal-cation diffusion.
The highly disordered multicomponent HEA matrix slows diffusion.
Slower diffusion in the disordered matrix promotes localized surface enrichment of reactive elements.
Selective oxidation of reactive elements produces a continuous, self-limiting protective scale.
Sluggish diffusion in the HEA matrix limits inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation migration.
Diffusion limitation by the HEA matrix stabilizes the protective oxide scale.
HEAs with sufficient reactive-element content will form thinner, more continuous, and more adherent scales than otherwise comparable HEAs with reduced reactive-element content.
HEAs with sufficient reactive-element content will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain than HEAs with reduced reactive-element content.
Reducing reactive-element content will cause formation of a porous, non-protective oxide scale.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 800–1100 °C in oxygen-rich environments.
Secondary alloying elements could modify oxidation rates and oxide microstructure.
Comparable scale continuity, density, protectiveness, and mass-gain kinetics in reduced-reactive-element and standard samples would falsify the proposed key mechanism.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says slowed diffusion promotes surface enrichment of reactive elements, whereas the mechanism says the same sluggish diffusion limits their outward migration. The hypothesis does not explain how sufficient reactive-element flux reaches the surface despite that limitation.
